evidenceAudit.scope: Recognition, work-up and long-term care of dementia in older adults in India at PHC, district and tertiary level: when to suspect, excluding delirium and depression, reversible causes, investigations, cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine, behavioural symptoms, caregiver support and referral, built on the ICMR Dementia STW (October 2019).
findings: Suspicion criteria, behavioural features, delirium and depression as alternatives, reversible causes (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, subdural haematoma, depression, normal pressure hydrocephalus, chronic meningitis), investigations by level, red flags (fever, rapid progression, seizures, head injury, alcoholism and falls), donepezil 5 mg then 10 mg, rivastigmine 1.5 mg twice daily titrated monthly to 6 mg twice daily, memantine 5 mg twice daily then 10 mg twice daily, galantamine 8 mg twice daily if others not tolerated, escitalopram 10 mg for depression, non-drug management of behaviour first, caregiver education and referral levels checked against the ICMR Dementia STW (October 2019).

Risperidone SmPC 4.1–4.4: 0.25 mg twice daily, increase by 0.25 mg twice daily no more often than every other day; optimum 0.5 mg twice daily, up to 1 mg twice daily; no longer than 6 weeks; halve doses in renal or hepatic impairment; increased mortality and about 3-fold cerebrovascular risk in elderly people with dementia; not for dementias other than Alzheimer.
unverifiedSections: The STW gives no screening tool cut-offs (MMSE or HMSE); none are shown.
The ICMR STW gives no antipsychotic dose; risperidone is taken from the UK summary of product characteristics (licensed only for short-term aggression in moderate to severe Alzheimer dementia).
Galantamine titration is incomplete in the STW (8 mg twice daily); the full titration and renal and hepatic limits are from the US label (Drugs.com).
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Dementia affects millions of older Indians, most undiagnosed, and is often dismissed as normal ageing. It is a progressive decline in memory and at least one other cognitive domain severe enough to affect daily function. The ICMR workflow asks primary care doctors to suspect it from the history given by a close caregiver, to rule out delirium and depression, to look for treatable causes (thyroid, B12, syphilis, HIV, subdural haematoma, normal pressure hydrocephalus), and to start a cholinesterase inhibitor for Alzheimer or mixed dementia, adding memantine in moderate to severe disease. Behavioural symptoms are managed first without drugs. Caregiver education, support and planning for palliative care are core. Alzheimer disease is the commonest type, followed by vascular and mixed dementia; the diagnosis is clinical and supported, not made, by tests.
keyMechanisms: Alzheimer disease: amyloid plaques and tau tangles with loss of cholinergic neurons.
Vascular dementia: multiple infarcts or small vessel disease; common in India with hypertension and diabetes.
Cholinesterase inhibitors increase acetylcholine; memantine blocks excess glutamate (NMDA) activity.
Delirium on top of dementia accelerates decline.

symptoms: Forgetfulness, repeating questions, getting lost (ICMR STW)
Difficulty with previously learned tasks (ICMR STW)
Apathy, aggression, sleep disturbance, hallucinations (ICMR STW)
Word-finding difficulty, misplacing objects and trouble with money or medicines
physicalSigns: Focal signs or gait disturbance (vascular, NPH)
Signs of hypothyroidism or B12 deficiency
Parkinsonism, fluctuating alertness or visual hallucinations (Lewy body dementia)
redFlags: Recent head injury; alcoholism and falls (subdural haematoma) (ICMR STW)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Acute onset over hours to days with fluctuating attention and often a medical cause; a 4AT or CAM assessment settles it (general practice).
Low mood, poor effort and 'don't know' answers on testing; improvement with antidepressant treatment settles it (ICMR STW).
Cognitive decline on testing with daily function preserved; caregiver history of independent function settles it.
Slowness, weight gain or neuropathy with cognitive decline; TSH and B12 levels settle it (ICMR STW).

differentials.condition: Chronic subdural haematoma or normal pressure hydrocephalus
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Falls, headache or gait apraxia with urinary incontinence; CT or MRI of the brain settles it (ICMR STW).
Younger onset or risk factors, rapid course; serum VDRL or TPHA then CSF testing, and HIV testing after counselling, settle it.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Decline in more than one cognitive domain along with functional decline, from baseline (ICMR STW).
Typical age, gradual progression, no focal signs.

ruleIn.testName: History from a close caregiver and cognitive examination
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Decline in memory and other domains with functional loss

clinicalManagement.title: Suspect and assess
actions: History from caregiver; exclude delirium and depression (ICMR STW).
Treat vascular risk factors and vision or hearing deficits (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Investigate
actions: Blood tests at PHC (blood count, biochemistry, liver, lipids, thyroid, VDRL, B12, vitamin D); neuroimaging and HIV testing after counselling at district level (ICMR STW).
Red flags or no response to adequate dose and duration of medicines: refer (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat
actions: Donepezil; rivastigmine or galantamine if not tolerated (ICMR STW).
Memantine for moderate to severe dementia (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Behavioural symptoms
actions: Find triggers (pain, infection, constipation, sleep, hearing loss); non-drug measures first (ICMR STW).
Avoid antipsychotics unless there is severe distress or risk of harm; in Alzheimer dementia, risperidone 0.25 mg twice daily for no more than 6 weeks (ICMR STW; SmPC).

clinicalManagement.title: Support
actions: Educate caregivers and enrol patient and caregiver in an ongoing support programme (ICMR STW); screen the caregiver for burden and depression (general practice).
Assess palliative care needs (ICMR STW); plan ahead for driving, finances and advance care (general practice).

vignette.text: Mr K, a 74-year-old retired railway clerk from Lucknow, is brought by his daughter, who says that over 2 years he has repeated questions, got lost returning from the market and stopped managing his pension. He now shouts at his wife in the evenings and once pushed her. He has hypertension and diabetes. There is no fever, no recent fall and no sudden change.

guidedApproach.title: Neurodegeneration and vascular injury
guidedApproach.prompt: What causes the decline, and why do the drugs help only a little?
guidedApproach.guidance: In Alzheimer disease, amyloid plaques and tau tangles cause loss of neurons and synapses, starting in the hippocampus and spreading to temporal and parietal cortex; this explains early memory loss and later language and visuospatial problems. Loss of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain reduces acetylcholine, which is why cholinesterase inhibitors give modest symptomatic benefit without changing the course. Glutamate excitotoxicity underlies the use of memantine. Vascular dementia results from strokes and small-vessel disease, often with stepwise decline and gait problems, and hypertension and diabetes are key modifiable risks in India. Mixed pathology is common in older people.

guidedApproach.title: History from the caregiver
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you recognise dementia and its subtype?
guidedApproach.guidance: Dementia is diagnosed when decline in memory and at least one other domain — language, attention, executive function or visuospatial skill — affects daily function. The history from a close caregiver is more reliable than the patient's own account. Ask how it began and progressed: gradual memory loss suggests Alzheimer disease, stepwise decline with focal signs suggests vascular dementia, early hallucinations and parkinsonism suggest Lewy body disease, and early personality change suggests frontotemporal dementia. Always look for delirium (acute, fluctuating) and depression, and for red flags such as fever, rapid progression, seizures or head injury that need urgent referral.

guidedApproach.title: Look for the reversible
guidedApproach.guidance: Basic tests at primary care look for treatable contributors: blood count, glucose, renal and liver function, electrolytes, TSH, vitamin B12, VDRL and HIV. These rarely reverse dementia but often make it worse when present. A brief cognitive screening test documents a baseline for later comparison; the STW names no specific tool, so use one validated in the patient's language. Neuroimaging (CT or MRI) at district level excludes subdural haematoma, tumours and normal pressure hydrocephalus and shows vascular disease. A rapid course or young onset needs specialist assessment for rarer causes.

guidedApproach.title: Drugs, behaviour and the caregiver
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you manage dementia step by step?
guidedApproach.guidance: Start donepezil 5 mg once daily for a month, then 10 mg, in Alzheimer or mixed dementia; use rivastigmine or galantamine if it is not tolerated. Add memantine 5 mg twice daily, rising to 10 mg twice daily, in moderate to severe disease. Treat depression with escitalopram 10 mg. Manage behavioural symptoms first by finding triggers — pain, constipation, infection, poor sleep — and with non-drug measures. If aggression in Alzheimer dementia persists with risk of harm, risperidone 0.25 mg twice daily (usually 0.5 mg twice daily, maximum 1 mg twice daily) may be used for no more than 6 weeks, accepting the increased stroke and mortality risk; avoid it in Lewy body and vascular dementia. Support and educate the caregiver.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 74-year-old man has 2 years of gradual memory decline, getting lost and inability to manage his money, reported by his daughter. He has hypertension and diabetes. Examination is non-focal. He is alert and attentive. TSH, B12, VDRL and HIV are normal, and CT shows mild atrophy.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.explanation: Antipsychotics are not treatment for cognitive decline and carry stroke and mortality risk.
There are no depressive symptoms described, so an antidepressant is not indicated.
Memantine is added for moderate to severe disease and is titrated from 5 mg twice daily.

options.text: No treatment; dementia is normal ageing
options.explanation: Dementia is not normal ageing and treatment and caregiver support are indicated.

options.text: Donepezil 5 mg once daily, increasing to 10 mg after 1 month
options.explanation: Correct. A cholinesterase inhibitor is first-line for Alzheimer or mixed dementia (ICMR STW).

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor in Alzheimer or mixed dementia.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Donepezil 5 mg, then 10 mg after a month.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 79-year-old woman with dementia became confused and agitated over 2 days, sleeping in the day and shouting at night. Her family says she was at her baseline last week. She has a temperature of 37.9 °C and dark, offensive urine. She has been constipated for 5 days.
boardQuestions.question: What is the best next step?

options.explanation: The maximum dose is 10 mg, and the change is acute, not progression.

options.text: Treat as delirium: look for and treat infection and constipation
options.explanation: Correct. Acute, fluctuating change in a person with dementia is delirium until proven otherwise (ICMR STW).
Antipsychotics are not first-line and the trigger has not been addressed.

options.text: Refer for MRI as an outpatient
options.explanation: This misses an acute medical cause that needs treatment now.
Two days of change with fever suggests delirium, not progression.

boardQuestions.keyPoint: Sudden change in dementia: think delirium and look for triggers.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 76-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer dementia has hit his wife repeatedly over 3 weeks despite pain relief, treatment of constipation, a structured routine and caregiver training. He takes donepezil 10 mg daily and has no parkinsonism or hallucinations. Creatinine and liver tests are normal. His wife is frightened and asks for help.
boardQuestions.question: Which treatment is most appropriate?

options.text: Risperidone 0.25 mg twice daily, titrated slowly, for no more than 6 weeks
options.explanation: Correct. Risperidone is licensed short term for persistent aggression in Alzheimer dementia after non-drug measures fail (SmPC 4.1–4.2).

options.text: Haloperidol 5 mg twice daily long term
options.explanation: High-dose, long-term typical antipsychotics cause severe parkinsonism and falls.
Regular benzodiazepines worsen confusion, sedation and falls in dementia.
This exceeds the 1 mg twice daily maximum and the 6-week limit (SmPC 4.2).
Stopping the cholinesterase inhibitor does not treat aggression and may worsen cognition.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Use antipsychotics only short term and at low dose in Alzheimer aggression.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Risperidone: 0.25 mg twice daily start, maximum 1 mg twice daily, 6 weeks.

patientEducation: Caregivers: routine, orientation cues, safety at home, wandering precautions.
Plan finances and decisions early while the person can take part.
lifestyleAndDiet: Physical activity, social engagement, control BP and diabetes, hearing aids and glasses.
mdtReferrals: Palliative care in advanced disease (ICMR STW)
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Follow up and monitor for side effects, red flags and danger signs (ICMR STW); monthly during titration, then every 3–6 months (general practice).

Acute onset or fluctuating attention?
Treat as delirium; find and treat the cause; reassess cognition once delirium resolves
Red flags: fever, rapid progression, seizures, head injury, focal signs?

Screen for depression (escitalopram 10 mg if depressed); PHC bloods incl. TSH, B12, VDRL; neuroimaging and HIV (after counselling) at district level
Reversible cause found?
Treat the cause and reassess cognition
Alzheimer or mixed dementia?
Donepezil 5 mg then 10 mg (or rivastigmine, galantamine)
Vascular: treat vascular risk factors; Lewy body or frontotemporal features: specialist referral, avoid antipsychotics
Moderate to severe?
Add memantine; caregiver support; non-drug care of behaviour
Continue; caregiver support; review every 3–6 months; refer if no response to adequate dose and duration

Look for triggers: pain, constipation, infection, retention, sleep, hearing or vision loss, new drugs; non-drug measures
Severe distress or risk of harm persisting despite this?
Continue non-drug care; support the caregiver; review
Alzheimer dementia without parkinsonism or Lewy body features?
Risperidone 0.25 mg twice daily, usual 0.5 mg twice daily, maximum 1 mg twice daily, for no more than 6 weeks (SmPC)
